newsitem.title: USA: U.S. health, religion groups seek quality in death.
newsitem.headline: U.S. health, religion groups seek quality in death.

text.p: A day before the Supreme Court takes up the issue, leading health, religious and retiree groups said Tuesday the whole debate over doctor-assisted suicide could be transformed if the quality of care for the dying was improved.

Although the 40-member coalition includes such prominent foes of assisted suicide as the American Medical Association, not all the members have formally opposed legalised assisted suicide in the two cases going before the Supreme Court Wednesday.

But they all agree the debate could be made largely irrelevant if people could count on end-of-life care that is "reliable, continuous, comprehensive and effective." They endorsed a 10-point programme for quality care for the dying including managing pain, treating depression, avoiding overuse of high-tech machinery and helping bereaved relatives.

Led by the American Geriatrics Society, the coalition includes the AMA, the American Association of Retired Persons (AARP), the American Cancer Society, B'nai Brith and the Catholic Health Association, among others.

"No one needs to be alone or in pain or to beg a doctor to put an end to misery," said Dr. Joanne Lynn, a board member of the geriatrics group and a George Washington University professor who led a landmark study on how people die.

The coalition said the American medical system, including Medicare and the managed care industry, should develop ways of monitoring the quality of end-of-life palliative care and making it more accessible.

Dr. Kathleen Foley, a pain management expert at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Centre, said about 1.6 million dying people a year would be good candidates for hospice care but only about 350,000 actually get it.

"No matter what one thinks of the merits of making it easier to commit suicide, we all must agree that public policy has a heavy obligation to provide care at the end of life," Lynn told a news conference. "We are talking about suicide as a society mainly because we have done so little to serve the dying and thus when we face death we see so few supportive options."
Lynn's study, published about a year ago, found that many people died alone, in pain and attached to machines. Their doctors often did not know their wishes for end-of-life care.

The U.S. high court Wednesday will hear two hours of arguments on whether mentally competent, terminally ill patients have a constitutional right to seek help from their doctors in committing suicide. A ruling is expected by July.

The dispute, which raises profound legal, moral and ethical questions, is among the most emotionally charged issues to reach the court since the landmark 1973 ruling in "Roe v. Wade" that women have a constitutional right to abortion.

A patient's right to refuse life support, resuscitation efforts or treatment for a fatal disease is widely accepted by courts and ethicists. But advocates of assisted suicide believe a patient should have the right to go a step further and actively decide when to put an end to suffering.
Critics say it is unnecessary and invites abuse.

Diane Coleman, a wheelchair-bound lawyer who is co-founder of an advocacy group called "Not Dead Yet," said a doctor faced with a depressed, able-bodied person offers suicide prevention but the same doctor faced with a depressed disabled person may offer suicide assistance.

"Research shows that physicians dramatically underestimate quality of life for people with disabilities, compared to our own assessment," she said at a separate news conference called by foes of assisted suicide.
